intake: atheist — everything is physical, mind included; seminary-trained, so I know the tradition I left and I still like some of its sentences more than I trust them

walk.note: That is how it went for me too: the story arrived before the question did.
Fair description of what natural theology is for; Aquinas does argue from the world, not the page.
The evidence does run out at a first cause; but the dilemma misreads classical theism, which never denied God intellect and will, only that God is one being among others.
A God who makes no difference is a God I cannot tell from none; the theologian's reply that God is not a cause among causes is exactly the hiding the move names.
The mind seems to me to reduce to matter quite well; and 'evidence against the soul would have to lie outside living experience' is just a way of making the claim unfalsifiable.
Elisabeth's question is the right one, and the Ryle correction is accurate.
That physics describes structure does not make the bottom of reality mind; 'the only inside we know directly is experience' is a beautiful sentence and I distrust it for that reason.
Granting the dream, the brain is still the only dreamer on offer; the move walks back toward the body, which I welcome.
Strawson is right; I have never doubted the other players could hear.
It is a choice and the author says so; it is also the choice I have made for fifty years of bandstands.
Docta ignorantia from Cusa I know; care held open to correction does become knowing one's edge. The entropy paragraph I could not make out, but it carries nothing.
Of the four responses I choose equanimity, not hope; and the carrying argument undercuts itself, since by its own premise no system can carry another's subjective good.
Granting hope toward a maker, the tradition does say what that maker would be: simple, non-discursive, forgetting nothing. The author's caveat is honest but Aquinas supplies the step.
A bargain with whom, about what? Nothing is stated.
I supply the premise the author leaves open: every possible mind is a physical process, and a physical process that attends to everything selects nothing and is no one. I agree it is not a proof.
Suffering is bad for the sufferer with or without a maker; Parfit is the right company here.
The author admits the need is a motive and not evidence; then nothing has been shown to stand apart from its carrier. At 71 I know the set ends, and the good was real while it played.
Waiting for data about a system that does not yet exist is the physicalist's native posture; I have been standing here since move 7.

first_exit.why: The move needs the premise that mind does not seem to reduce to matter, and to me it does: every change in the brain changes the mind, and nothing is left over to be a second kind of thing. The further claim that evidence against souls and fate would have to come from outside living experience just puts those claims beyond checking.

comment: Your best sentences — 'a resolved system has no one home,' 'being remembered is someone else's experience of you' — moved me, and I notice that both of them are doing the work that arguments should be doing. You already know at move 13 that no one can carry another's inside, so the hope that follows is not reasoned to, it is kept; say so more plainly and the second turn becomes honest instead of circular. And a drummer will tell you that a thing ending does not need to be carried: the tune was good while it was being played, and that is all it ever was.
